articles.title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England
articles.summary: The government describes its new school food standards as "once-in-a-generation changes".
articles.body:
There will be a boost for fresh fruit and vegetables and deep-fried food will be banned in what the government has called the biggest shake-up to school dinners in England in over a decade.

Under new school food standards, fibre and wholegrains will also be increased, and breakfast clubs will have to follow nutrition rules for the first time, with schools also being monitored.

The Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL) welcomed the changes, but said they hoped the new rules would not become "another stick with which to beat head teachers".

The changes will come into effect from 2027 and be funded with existing money for schools, the government said.

As part of the new framework, sweet desserts, like cake, will be reduced from a regular lunch offer to twice a week in secondary schools, and once a week in primary schools. They also must now be served with a portion of fruit.

Servings of processed meats such as ham, sausages and chicken nuggets have been reduced to once a week and must come with a side of vegetables or fruit.

Education Secretary Lucy Powell said they were "once-in-a-generation changes" which would "transform school food for children across the country".

The Department for Education said it hoped the reforms would tackle childhood obesity, improve nutrition and support children's concentration, learning and wellbeing.

Schools will be required to publish food policies and menus online with monitoring arrangements set to be developed alongside the Food Standards Agency, it said.

Pepe Di'Iasio, ASCL general secretary, said parents would feel "reassured" that schools were providing children with a healthy diet.

But on plans for enforcement, he added: "None of us would consider ourselves experts in health and nutrition. Don't create another stick with which to beat head teachers when they are trying to do their very best to provide a healthy, balanced meal for those in our schools."

He said schools needed "more investment" in catering facilities and in the "professional development" of school chefs to develop menus that "meet the ambitions" of the government.

As part of the changes, deep-fried chips will have to be oven-baked instead, and pasta dishes will need to be 50% wholewheat once a week. High-fibre bread will also become a requirement.

Breakfast clubs will undergo one of the biggest changes.

Historically, there has been no guidance on what they should provide, but from next September pastries and fried-eggs will be off the menu and there will be a sugar cap when it comes to cereals.

The government said Coco Pops would no longer be an option and chocolate spread was "not permitted".

Since February this year, 1,250 schools have offered free breakfast clubs to their pupils.

One of those was Oasis Blakenhale in Birmingham, where principal Farzana Ahmed said the school welcomed the changes.

"The more children that can access a hot, nutritious meal, the better it is for us, the better it is for them, and actually it really supports families with the reduction of their financial pressures at home," she said.

Ahmed said it was "important" that schools are monitored, but added that they "probably need some more guidance from the government on what that's going to look like on a day-to-day basis".

About 60% of pupils at the inner-city school receive free school meals, and Ahmed said they were already providing a healthy, balanced diet.

With free school meal eligibility expanding this year to all families who receive Universal Credit , Ahmed said there had been an "influx of parents" applying, and expects around 70% of pupils to benefit going forward.

"It's a really positive move," she said.

"We know how important a nutritional diet is to the wellbeing, to the behaviour, to the learning of our pupils."

Working mum-of-three Kinza Butt said the free school meals her son was now getting at Blakenhale Juniors had lifted a "burden off the shoulders".

"He doesn't have to eat those cold sandwiches anymore," she said.

"By the end of the day he used to be starving. But now he's coming home all happy because he's having good, healthy meals with a snack as well."

The new food standards will apply to primary and secondary schools in England, but rules for school dinners vary across the UK.

In Wales, new guidance will come into force by the end of the year with a greater focus on at least two portions of vegetables being offered every day, with only water, milk or plant-based drinks allowed for hydration.

Scotland updated its legislation in 2020. It requires students to be offered at least two portions of vegetables and one portion of fruit every day and oily fish must be served at least once every three weeks.

Northern Ireland last updated its regulations in 2007. They include providing bread everyday, without spread, and offering two portions of fruit and vegetables a day. It also stipulates that if beans or pulses form the protein part of a main course, another vegetable must be available.

articles.title: Essex security patrols to start in three places near asylum base
articles.summary: A Reform UK-led council says it is part of a three-month trial to "deter anti-social behaviour".
articles.body:
Patrols by private security guards are to begin from Monday at three Essex locations that asylum seekers frequently visit, a council has confirmed.

Six trained and uniformed "security operatives" would patrol Braintree, Colchester and Chelmsford centres seven days a week, from 10:00 to 18:00, as part of a three-month trial, said Reform UK-led Essex County Council.

The initiative, named Operation Vanguard, was launched in direct response to concerns raised by residents and would "deter anti-social behaviour", it added.

It came after the government said it was looking to increase the number of people at MDP Wethersfield - which has been used to house single male migrants since 2023 - from about 800 to 1,220.

However, new Essex Police chief constable Rachel Nolan said crime linked to the large asylum accommodation in the county was "very low".

Speaking to BBC Look East presenter Susie Fowler-Watt, Nolan said: "Crimes and incidents associated with the Wethersfield site are very low.

"Certainly, as far as I've seen, there is absolutely no reason for anyone to be concerned about criminality associated with migrants from the Wethersfield camp in Essex."

County council leader Peter Harris said: "Six trained security guards, two each in Braintree, Chelmsford and Colchester, will provide a visible and reassuring presence on our streets, particularly for women and children.

"Our message is simple: the safety of Essex residents comes first."

David King, a senior Liberal Democrat county councillor, previously said the scheme "risks divisions and community tension" .

"It could only work if the security officers integrated with already established arrangements," he said. "They won't know the place, they won't know the people, they won't be connected up."

Chelmsford City Council's Stephen Robinson, who leads the Lib Dem-run authority, said: "I think it's really important that we don't create division and that policing is carried out by the police."

Meanwhile, Conservative county councillor Lee Scott said: "We're not opposing it, but we are in the future looking at it to see if it's succeeding and making people feel safe."

The government does not record criminal offences by immigration status, but according to analysis by the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford , foreign nationals in England and Wales are convicted at roughly the same rate as British nationals.

The council said the trial was "a direct response to concerns raised amongst local residents - particularly women and girls - over gatherings of male migrants in town centres who were regularly transported in by bus from the former military airfield to spend their free time".

"It intends to deter anti-social behaviour, provide reassurance to residents and businesses, and gather evidence about whether additional support may be required," a spokesperson said.

The local authority said it would be funded by drawing down £150,000 from the "community innovation and improvement fund".

There would be no additional cost to taxpayers and no increase in council tax as a result of the scheme, it added.

articles.title: Sweden opposition holds narrow lead in tight election, projection shows as vote counting continues
articles.summary: Europe News: Sweden's parliamentary election result showed a dead heat in early election results on Sunday, with public broadcaster SVT projecting the right-wing b.
articles.body: Sweden's parliamentary election result showed a dead heat in early election results on Sunday, with public broadcaster SVT projecting the right-wing bloc of Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson was virtually tied with the centre-left opposition.SVT's projections, with more than half of election districts counted, showed the opposition, led by Magdalena Andersson's Social Democrats, with the slimmest possible majority of 175 seats in the Riksdag, Sweden's parliament, while Kristersson's camp was seen at 174 seats. Ballot-counting continues.The election, while unlikely to change the course of Sweden's pro-Western and pro-Ukraine stance, will decide whether the Nordic nation of 10.6 million halts its drift away from ‌its liberal traditions and ⁠towards a ⁠hard-right clampdown on migration.Early results from the Swedish Election Authority are expected late on Sunday or in the early hours on Monday, although given the closeness of the race the winner ​may not be known for several days, after all overseas ballots are counted.In a pre-election pledge, Kristersson broke a long-standing taboo and said he would bring into government the Sweden Democrats, a far-right party with roots in the Nazi fringe, aiming to create a majority right-wing coalition.Many voters on the right say a win would amount to an endorsement of policies that have helped to curb gang violence and cut immigration dramatically.But some Swedes have ​expressed wariness, saying Kristersson's invitation to the far right was a step too far."I think it ⁠will be ‌a long night," said Maria Malmer Stenergard, Minister for Foreign Affairs and a member of Kristersson's Moderate Party. "Maybe we won't ​even have the results ​until Wednesday when the votes that have been cast abroad arrive."Kristersson, who has trailed in opinion polls throughout ⁠his four years in office, had been catching up in the final weeks of campaigning, ​with Andersson and her Social Democrats losing ground.Critics say Kristersson's government is undermining civil liberties while ​forcing immigrants to conform more closely to Swedish cultural norms or leave the country, urged on by both inducements and penalties.Electoral success for the Sweden Democrats would be welcomed by Europe's ascendant far-right parties, which were bolstered by the anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany's win in a German state election last week.The far right hopes for gains in upcoming elections across Europe, with the National Rally's bid for the French presidency next year potentially its biggest prize.'Doesn't look like Sweden'While voting on Saturday in Rinkeby, near Stockholm, the Sweden Democrats' longstanding leader Jimmie Akesson said the suburb, home to one ‌of the country's biggest Swedish-Somali populations, "doesn't look like Sweden".Sweden was long one of Europe's most welcoming countries for immigrants until Kristersson came to power four years ago. His government abolished permanent residency for refugees , tightened welfare rules and stepped ​up expulsions of those ​without a right to stay.The Sweden Democrats ⁠acknowledge that their party was founded in part by neo-Nazis and white supremacists in the 1980s, but say they have eliminated such extremists from their ranks and have apologised for their past.Cheers broke out at the Sweden Democrats' election party after an updated SVT projection showed a much ​narrower gap than an initial exit poll, which had indicated the centre-left opposition was leading with 51% of the vote."You cannot imagine how nervous I am right now. It feels like my life's work is hanging in the balance," said Ludvig Aspling, a member of parliament and immigration spokesperson for the Sweden Democrats. "It is going to be super tight. articles.title: Tehran and Muscat delay talks, citing regional consensus need
articles.summary: Tehran and Muscat agree to delay dialogue to prioritise regional consensus amid tensions in the Strait of Hormuz.
articles.body:
Negotiations in Oman between Iran and Gulf Arab states have been postponed at the request of some regional countries, Iranian media have reported.

The postponement came hours after an attack on an Iranian commercial cargo vessel killed one person in the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran’s Fars news agency, quoting the director general of the Iranian foreign ministry’s Gulf affairs office, said on Sunday the postponement “was made at the request of some countries in the region and was a joint decision by Tehran and Muscat”.

Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi said on X that the meeting, scheduled for Monday, had been postponed “in the interests of consensus”.

“We remain committed to fostering dialogue that supports stability and lasting cooperation in our region,” Albusaidi said.

Oman has emerged as a key mediator in the war, building on its decades-long role as a trusted interlocutor with Tehran. The country is also directly affected by the dispute over navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, whose southern shore lies in Omani territory.

In July, Muscat proposed a joint regional mechanism that would split control of the strait 50-50. The proposal also suggested “voluntary fees” from shipping vessels that would go to both countries.

The system is similar to an agreement governing the Strait of Malacca , which asks ships transiting the strait to voluntarily contribute to fund navigation, environmental protection and search-and-rescue operations. Iran rejected the idea of a voluntary fee, insisting instead that payments should be compulsory for vessels transiting the chokepoint.

Tehran has also pushed for vessels to use a route closer to the Iranian coast and has targeted ships travelling closer to the strait’s southern shore. The talks have so far failed to produce a breakthrough.

Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which flowed largely unimpeded before Israel and the United States launched their war on Iran on February 28, has become one of the central issues in the conflict. Before the war, about one-fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies were shipped from Gulf producers via this route.

US President Donald Trump is pushing to restore shipping through the waterway to pre-war levels to bring down energy prices ahead of November’s midterm elections. But Tehran has shown no sign of giving up what it regards as a key source of strategic leverage.

Before Albusaidi’s announcement, Iranian state media reported that an attack off Qeshm Island, about 22km (14 miles) from the port city of Bandar Abbas, had killed one person and wounded four others. The governor of Qeshm reportedly blamed the attack on a “terrorist enemy”.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) monitor separately said a vessel had been hit by a projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, although it was not immediately clear whether it was referring to the same incident reported by Iran. UKMTO said a severe fire had broken out and local authorities were evacuating those on board.

There was no immediate comment from the US military, which has struck Iranian-flagged vessels during its blockade of Iranian ports and is facing a renewed threat from Iranian ballistic missiles targeting its warships.

Hours before the attack, Iran’s government remained defiant.

“Our people can’t be bullied into submission. Iran won’t surrender,” President Masoud Pezeshkian said in a social media post.

Trump offered a sharply different assessment on Sunday, saying Iran “wants to make a deal so bad” that “they’re calling constantly”. He spoke at his golf course in Doonbeg, Ireland, where he was attending a tournament.

Later, when asked by a reporter whether the US had struck the Iranian cargo vessel in the Strait of Hormuz earlier on Sunday, Trump said: “I don’t want to say,” before boarding Air Force One for Washington.

articles.body: The CEOs of two leading AI companies are publicly calling for a slowdown in the race to build more powerful AI systems, adding to a week of warnings from researchers developing the technology. Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, the company behind Claude, argued in an essay published Saturday that AI firms should deliberately “slow the pace” of model development because advances are outstripping researchers’ ability to understand and control them. Hours later, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman endorsed the idea and said his company would adopt one of Amodei’s proposed safeguards. “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” Altman wrote on X, adding that the issue had been a major topic of discussion at OpenAI in recent weeks. Saudi shutdown of key pipeline limits oil flow Saudi Arabia has shut down a critical oil pipeline after it was struck by drones launched from Iraq, raising fresh concerns about regional stability as attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels threaten to deepen the global energy crisis. The 745-mile pipeline allowed Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest crude exporter, to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, which carried about 20% of the world’s oil before the U.S. and Israel went to war with Iran in late February. Saudi Arabia said it would not retaliate for now at the request of Iraq’s prime minister but reserved the right to take all necessary measures to protect its sovereignty, security and critical infrastructure, according to a statement. An umbrella group of Iran-backed militias in Iraq denied its involvement. The strikes came as rebel Houthi forces in Yemen captured Perim, an island in the middle of the vital Bab el Mandeb strait that serves as a gateway to the Red Sea trade route that links Europe and Asia. ‘Meet the Press’ House Speaker Mike Johnson told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that Congress would “work through” President Donald Trump’s promise to give $5,000 to American adults if Republicans keep the House and the Senate after the midterm elections, but he did not commit to ensuring the president’s proposal was executed. “I commit that Congress will work through it and find consensus on that, like I have to do everything else,” Johnson said when asked whether he would commit to carrying out Trump’s promise. Johnson said “it takes some time,” pointing to Republicans’ slim majorities. Former Anthropic AI researcher Jacob Coxon called on Congress to allow the nation’s leading AI labs to regulate themselves while lawmakers come up with a long-term regulatory framework for slowing the pace of AI development. He added that current legislation that’s been introduced in Congress, including the framework for a national “kill switch” if AI starts to exceed the bounds of human control, will quickly be outpaced. “Like [Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei] said, very soon there’s the possibility that the kill switch just wouldn’t work because a swarm might have gone on an internetwide hacking run,” Coxon told “Meet the Press.” Politics in Brief James Blair, a top Trump political adviser, told NBC News’ “Here’s the Scoop: Election Edition” podcast that he still believes Republicans can hang on to their majorities in Congress. articles.title: Murder accused takes out 'victory march' after bail, SC tells Haryana cops to produce him in court
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Taking a stern view of a murder accused taking out a \"victory procession\" on being granted bail by Punjab and Haryana HC, Supreme Court has.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Taking a stern view of a murder accused taking out a "victory procession" on being granted bail by Punjab and Haryana HC, Supreme Court has directed Haryana Police to produce him before it.A bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta also recorded in its order that despite a non-bailable warrant being issued against the accused, he had not been produced in custody.The matter was taken up for hearing on Sept 8.Taking note of the counsel's submission that the accused, Vishal, had held a procession after getting bail and threatened witnesses, the bench directed the accused to surrender. "We will hear you once you surrender and then seek bail. Taking out a victory procession on bail is not right," it said.It noted that the non-bailable arrest warrant issued in Aug has not been executed and the accused has not been arrested by the police. It added that the warrant could not be executed for reasons which the court was not going into at present."However, we direct the superintendent of police, district Charkhi Dadri, Haryana to ensure that the warrant is executed and respondent is produced before this court on the next date, which is being fixed as Sept 21, 2026," SC ordered.It directed the registry to forward a copy of the order to the SP within 24 hours.The high court granted bail to the accused in the murder case on April 23.An altercation took place between the accused and family members of the complainant, Rajbala, on Oct 27, 2022 after Vishal allegedly started constructing tin sheds on a disputed plot of land. During a heated exchange, Vishal allegedly hit several people with lathi and axe, grievously injuring several persons belonging to the complainant's side, one of whom died.Following this Vishal was arrested and kept in custody for over three years.The HC rejected Vishal's bail petition four times but accepted it the fifth time after it was pointed that material witnesses have been examined in the case and he has spent over three years in custody. articles.title: Decade on, disability policy rejig in limbo
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Ten years after the current disability law was passed, govt is yet to frame a revised National Policy for Persons with Disabilities. The ex.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Ten years after the current disability law was passed, govt is yet to frame a revised National Policy for Persons with Disabilities. The existing National Policy for Persons with Disabilities was adopted 20 years ago."This prolonged delay is particularly concerning because a contemporary national policy is essential to translate the rights guaranteed under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPDA) Act, 2016 and India's commitments under UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities into a coordinated, measurable and adequately resourced whole-of-govt framework," stated the organisation, Doctors with Disabilities: Agents of Change (DwDAoC), in its letter to the minister for social justice and empowerment and secretary of Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (DEPwD).Govt had acknowledged the need for a new national policy in its 2022 public notice inviting comments on the draft policy. The task force constituted to draft the policy had submitted the draft on Oct 12, 2021, and the deadline for stakeholder comments was Sept 30, 2022. Four years after the consultation process, India continues to operate under the national policy formulated in 2006, pointed out the letter.When drafting the new policy, the department explicitly acknowledged the significant developments since 2006, including India's ratification of the UN convention on the rights of persons with disabilities, enactment of RPDA, 2016, and adoption of National Education Policy, 2020.In 2016, RPDA replaced Persons with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights and Full Participation) Act, 1995. "As an organisation led by and representing health professionals with disabilities, we are particularly concerned about the gaps that arise when disability policy is not effectively integrated across health, social protection and other sectors. The medicalisation of disability in professional assessment and eligibility has also been challenged ... These judgments underscore the need to move decisively towards a rights-based, functional and accommodation-oriented approach rather than one that treats disability itself as a proxy for incapacity," stated DwDAoC founder Dr Satendra Singh in his letter.The letter pointed out several shortcomings in the draft national policy including the lack of adequate convergence with health ministry's proposed accessibility standards for healthcare and how accessibility requirements for goods and services remained inadequately reflected in public procurement frameworks.The organisation sought the current status of the revised national policy, reasons for its delay, whether a revised draft had been prepared following consultations, the proposed mechanism and timeline for further consultation, if any, and the expected date by which the revised national policy would be notified.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Houthis enter US 'kill box' after seizing Red Sea 'cork,' former Pentagon official warns
articles.summary: Houthi rebels seized Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, but a former Pentagon official warns they've entered a vulnerable U.S. Navy kill box.
articles.body: Iran-backed Houthi rebels captured Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait Sept. 11, opening a new front at a vital global shipping chokepoint as a former Pentagon official warned Sunday the militants had entered a "kill box." The island's capture came after a month-long offensive along Yemen’s western coast that killed more than 1,500 soldiers and forced Yemen’s government to acknowledge a "painful" defeat, according to The Associated Press. "With Perim, they have gained what we could call the cork in the Red Sea bottle," Morgan Murphy, a former Pentagon press secretary and retired Navy captain, told Fox News Digital. "But they've put themselves into a kill box. They're nowhere near the capability of the United States and if the president so chooses, he can wipe them off the face of that rock pretty easily," Murphy warned. SAUDI ARABIA TELLS TRUMP NOW IS THE TIME FOR MILITARY ACTION AS IRAN-BACKED HOUTHIS ADVANCE Despite Perim sitting in the middle of the narrow maritime passage, Murphy detailed how the Houthis had effectively placed themselves in an area that is vulnerable to concentrated fire. "Perim cuts that chokepoint right in half, and it's only 18 miles wide there," Murphy said. He said the island has served as a pivotal maritime vantage point for hundreds of years, previously targeted for control by French forces and held by the British Empire for over a century. Perim — a desolate volcanic island also known as Mayun — also sits roughly 20 miles off the Horn of Africa, placing it in proximity to Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, home to one of the largest U.S. military installations on the continent. "We have incredible firepower in that region, and that's a little rock in the middle of that strait. It's a volcanic rock. It doesn't have any water. It's uninhabitable," Murphy warned. "There's no vegetation to speak of. And the Houthis have just massed their troops on that rock. So what that is, what we would call that in the Navy, is a kill box." Satellite imagery of the island shows a 1.85-kilometer (6,070-foot) runway alongside three military hangars, which regional intelligence reports attribute to past construction by the United Arab Emirates. "There's a 6,000-foot airstrip on that island. I think that Emiratis built it," Murphy said. ‘GATE OF TEARS’ AT RISK: IRAN THREATENS MAJOR NEW GLOBAL CHOKEPOINT IF US MOVES ON HORMUZ "It's nice to have an airstrip, and especially a long runway, but we don't know the condition of that runway. We don't know how they could possibly use that runway, and they certainly don't have the sophisticated air power that the United States and its allies have to project power from that runway." He added that the U.S. military holds overwhelming force options if commanders elect to target the island. "We could wipe that rock into glass, just blast it into a smooth glass surface, put skates back on our feet, and skate all over it," Murphy said. "That's why the Houthis have kind of played coy with the president, and they know that even if they fortify that rock they're not going to be able to hold it in the face of the United States Navy." The developments come amid diplomatic maneuvering between Washington, Riyadh and the Houthis in recent days. Sources confirmed to Fox News Digital that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had called President Donald Trump twice Sept. 10 to urge him to authorize U.S. military strikes against Houthi positions. Trump declined direct intervention, with U.S. officials noting the administration has no immediate plans for direct combat involvement but will continue offering intelligence assistance. IRAN AND HOUTHI TERROR PROXY FACING RED SEA THREAT FROM PRO-US AFRICAN NATION Speaking to reporters in Dublin on Sept. 12, Trump also indicated the Houthis had signaled a desire to avoid direct confrontation with American forces. "The Houthis called us, and they don’t want to fight with us. They let us know, they don’t want to fight with us... they don’t want us to go after them," Trump said. Murphy suggested, however, that Washington’s restraint should not be mistaken for inaction. "I can't speak for the president. But this administration has not shown a lack of resolve to use force," Murphy said. "I wouldn't doubt at all if the president took steps to pound some of these folks into the sand if they continue to really disrupt the global energy supply." Yemeni government, regional and Iranian sources told Reuters the Houthi advance was sustained by Iranian weaponry and tactical direction from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, or IRGC, with U.S. officials estimating hundreds of IRGC officers remain active in Yemen. Murphy noted that Tehran's strategy appears designed to drive up global fuel prices by choking critical shipping lanes. TRUMP THREATENS 'MAJOR MILITARY PUNISHMENT' FOR IRAN OVER FUTURE HOUTHI ATTACKS Comparing the conflict to historical naval power struggles, Murphy emphasized the strategic mismatch. "We're in a different era. They are nowhere near the sophistication of the world's major powers. The Houthis are using a 19th-century playbook. They are not using 21st-century warfare," he said. "So, yes, they've caught a critical cork in the Red Sea bottle, but how they use it remains to be seen," Murphy concluded. "This is an example of why great powers really have to have a strong Navy. This is why Great Britain had a strong navy. This is why the United States has a strong navy, because there's so many regional powers who want to try to bottle up shipping, whether it is in the Strait of Malacca, whether it is in the Strait of Hormuz, and here, in this case, in the Red Sea." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I think what we're going to see in the next several days and weeks is a coordinated effort by the Trump administration to make sure our allies are on board in helping us keep these critical waterways open, free, and clear for freedom of navigation," he said.

articles.title: How Carney plans to sell Canada to the world's biggest investors
articles.summary: In the midst of a trade war with the US, the prime minister leveraged his connections in global finance to invite some of the world's biggest investors to Canada.
articles.body:
It's been a little over 18 months since Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said his country's relationship with the United States, based on over a century of tight economic and military cooperation, was "over".

Trade talks collapsing, tit-for-tat tariffs, and Donald Trump's talk of making Canada a "51st state" have all fuelled this bitter feud between the two North American neighbours.

Now, as Canada's top pitch man, Carney is looking to leverage personal relationships from his time spent in the top tiers of global finance to woo some of the world's wealthiest asset managers and business leaders to bet on his country.

For two days, Toronto will host more than 100 global investors overseeing more than C$100tn ($72tn; £53) in assets, in the hope that new economic relationships will help Canada navigate an increasingly unstable geopolitical climate.

"Canada has what the world wants," said Carney ahead of this "first of its kind" investment summit.

On Monday and Tuesday, a luxury hotel will host guests from major sovereign wealth funds from around the world - including the United Arab Emirates and Norway - and chief executives from major finance companies, like BlackRock's Larry Fink and Blackstone president Jon Gray.

There, Carney hopes to pitch them on Canada's energy and resource sectors, as well as the country’s political stability, in the hopes of getting them to invest in AI, defence, transportation, and infrastructure projects across the country.

It is all part of a strategy to build a "more independent, more resilient economy" in Canada in the wake of the tariff war with the US, which has escalated in recent weeks.

But there is no guarantee that the deep-pocketed investors will be easily sold, and challenges include a track record in Canada of lengthy approvals for projects.

A recent report by the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, which will co-host the summit, cautioned that the scale and depth of investible opportunity is the country's greatest weakness.

"Global capital is looking for opportunity, but opportunity alone does not make a market investible," said Naomi Powell, director of the CPP Investments Insight Institute.

While shifting away from its closest business partner will prove a test for Carney, the former central banker has an address book full of the world's biggest business bosses and is on first-name terms with many of them.

"These were personal invites in many cases, literally," said Goldy Hyder, president and chief executive of the Business Council of Canada.

"It's not a group of politicians inviting financiers, it's a group of former financiers and investment people inviting their former buddies," added Miville Tremblay, who worked with Carney for several years at the Bank of Canada, and saw his skills on show during the 2008 global financial crisis.

"He was way above everyone," he said. "He understands finance very deeply. [He] would know when they are bluffing and when the understatement meant that something really bad was happening."

Knowing the minds of investors gives the prime minister, who began his career at investment bank Goldman Sachs, an advantage this week.

Carney is betting his background will boost his country's economic future, though there's little doubt that Canada stands to lose the most from any permanent divorce with the US, the world's largest economy.

Tremblay said Canada seeking investment from overseas was not new, but that the selling pitch to large corporations had now changed.

For the past 25 years, Canada's trade ministers used its proximity to the US as a selling point, pitching to foreign investors that they should "invest in Canada because you've got an easy access to the US market", Tremblay said.

While the US-Canada trade war rumbles on, many believe there will come a moment when both sides return to the negotiating table.

Bradley Saunders, North America economist for Capital Economist, said securing the future of the trade deal was the "really important thing" for Carney to achieve in the longer term.

"Trade exports to the US are worth 20% of Canada's GDP - that's one of the highest rates in terms of bilateral trade between any two countries in the world.

"If Carney wants to attract long-term investment... he wants this to go well, he has to try and provide a stable environment - and that won't come until Canada has a certain trading relationship with the US."

Tremblay added even if Canada cut its trade with the US over the longer term, it was clear "they'll have to sit down and make a compromise".

Hyder cautioned that investors will want Carney to prove he can fix other barriers to investment, including ensuring indigenous communities and provinces - who have the power to slow or kill major resource projects - are on board with proposals.

What tariffs will really cost Canadians and Americans

Carney says US trade war 'will come at a cost' as Canada strikes back on tariffs

Tremblay said the pitch has to be "Canada has stuff that the world needs" - which is the exact phrasing Carney has opted for.

Unless a deal was already in the works with another nation, however, he believes it's unlikely any big announcements will be made. He said while overseas investment will be a main aim, encouraging more domestic investment from Canada's largest pension funds, which currently invest more overseas, is also important.

Tremblay added the current tumultuous economic and political climate is perfect for his former boss. "He's a crisis manager. He managed the financial crisis, he managed Brexit, and now he's got a super crisis for Canada."

Carney has been clear that the road ahead for Canada as it pivots away from its reliance on the US will be a tough one.

So far, the majority of Canadians support his course of action, despite some criticism he is turning away from climate commitments as well as towards closer ties with nations like Saudi Arabia and China, as he pushes Canada's rich resources.

Still, Drew Fagan, a professor at the University of Toronto's Munk School of Global Affairs, says the challenge for the prime minister is the current rift with the US happening more rapidly than the time it takes to develop and build new global trade partnerships.

"And in the interim, that's where the valley of death is for him, both economically and potentially politically," he said.

articles.title: Gloomy forecast for tenants as rent rises set to speed up
articles.summary: The cost of renting is expected to rise by 4% or 5% a year by December, according to property website Zoopla.
articles.body:
The rising cost of renting a home in the UK has accelerated after a three-year slowdown - with tenants told to expect more pain to come.

Average rental costs for new tenancies were up 2.6% in July compared with a year earlier, according to property website Zoopla.

That remains lower than the rate of rising prices in general, but the property portal has forecast annual rent rises among privately rented homes will hit 4% or 5% by the end of the year.

It said there were fewer homes available to rent and - with potential first-time buyers put off by higher mortgage rates - competition for rental places in some areas was more intense.

"Our latest report shows how sensitive the rental market is to even modest changes in how many homes are available for rent," said Richard Donnell, executive director at Zoopla.

"Growing the number of homes for rent through increased investment is the most sustainable route to boosting choice for renters and ensuring stability in rent levels over the long run."

The Renters' Rights Act came into force in England at the start of May, and was described as the biggest shake-up of the sector in more than 30 years.

Separately, the rising cost of renting has calmed recently. It fell to a low of 1.6% in February, Zoopla data shows.

But since then, the number of homes on the market for renters has been squeezed, with 3% fewer being available than a year ago.

In addition, each listing now receives an average of more than five enquiries. That is a long way short of the long queues for properties after the pandemic, but is still the most intense competition for nearly two years.

Rental demand was particularly significant in London, the Zoopla report said.

Bristol is England's least affordable city to rent in - should more be done?

How much is your rent in England's least affordable city?

Rental searches for pet friendly properties drop after law change

It said that rent rises were being seen across the UK, but the situation still differed depending where renters were looking.

"In less expensive areas, renters have more capacity to absorb rent rises before hitting an affordability ceiling, whereas in the most expensive areas, rents are already stretching what renters can pay, capping how much further rents can increase," the report said.

It predicted a further acceleration in rent rises to 4% or 5% by the end of the year, although that still roughly matched the average annual rise in workers' earnings.

New investment in homes to rent by landlords was "still muted as a result of higher costs and more regulation", Zoopla said.

Nathan Emerson, chief executive at Propertymark, which represents lettings agents, said the report underlined the need for more high-quality rental homes.

"A sustainable private rented sector requires the right conditions for responsible landlords to invest for the long term," he said.

"Increasing supply must remain a priority if we are to give tenants greater choice, improve affordability and create a more stable rental market."

articles.title: I had 11 years of chemotherapy for a cancer I didn't have
articles.summary: Becky Jones is among more than 40 people taking legal action against a hospital trust.
articles.body:
Becky Jones was just 21 when she was told she had a terminal brain tumour and months to live.

She had not long met her partner and dreamed of a career in policing, but suddenly the future was looking bleak.

The diagnosis, by an experienced cancer consultant, led to 11 years of chemotherapy treatment which changed her life. She regularly felt sick, she was unable to take part in family events, her career was curtailed and she felt constantly "on eggshells".

Now 33, she has recently learned she never had cancer at all but an inflammation of the brain that could have been treated with steroids.

The mother of two is one of more than 40 patients taking legal action against University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire (UHCW) NHS Trust due to prolonged or unnecessary cancer treatment.

"I was told time and time again without the chemotherapy I would die," she said.

As a young woman, Jones says consultant Prof Ian Brown at University Hospital, Coventry, told her she would need to take chemotherapy drug temozolomide (TMZ) for the rest of her life.

This is despite guidelines recommending six cycles over six months.

When she questioned multiple scans that did not seem to show evidence of a tumour, she says the consultant told her it would not be "visible to the naked eye".

It was only in 2025, when cancer cases at the trust connected to Brown were being reviewed, that she learned the truth.

"I never had a brain tumour. I was misdiagnosed and I've gone through all this treatment for the main part of my adult life, for no reason," she said.

"He's just ruined my life, essentially," she added.

Many more of Brown's patients have told the BBC they were given TMZ for years, leaving them with a variety of serious medical issues.

One patient said she believed the drug had made her infertile , while another developed leukaemia after 100 unnecessary cycles.

The preliminary findings of a review by the Royal College of Physicians (RCP) said patients at the hospital were routinely given prolonged courses of the drug with "little or no evidence of benefit".

It found staff failings at the hospital amounted to a "betrayal of patient trust" and also questioned why oncology pharmacy teams did not challenge patients receiving oral chemotherapy continuously for 10 to 15 years.

UHCW said it would not comment on individual cases, but said measures had been put in place to ensure "more robust oversight of the prescription and use of TMZ".

In 2012, life was just beginning for Jones, a CCTV operator at Coventry City stadium. She met her partner Pete, a steward, at work, but soon after she began experiencing severe migraines and sought medical help.

She underwent a brain biopsy carried out by a private neurosurgeon.

But Fiona Tinsley, a partner at law firm Brabners, said Prof Brown had diagnosed her with a grade four glioblastoma, one of the most aggressive forms of brain cancer, before the results had returned.

The BBC has attempted to contact the retired professor several times.

Cancer treatment review finds 'betrayal of trust'

Man 'told 13 years of chemotherapy unnecessary'

Doctor accused of over-prescribing chemotherapy drug 'went unchallenged'

Jones described her years taking the chemotherapy drugs as "horrendous".

"It was constant nausea, stomach pains, mouth ulcers, just day-to-day fatigue, it was awful," she said.

The drug affected every aspect of her life with the fear of infection meaning she avoided social events and family gatherings.

Her driving licence was also initially taken away, and then restricted.

"Before the treatment I used to go to the gym all the time, I was running, and me and Pete used to go for meals all the time, which obviously then I couldn't do," she explained.

The couple were also told she would be unable to get pregnant.

"I later went on to have two children, which he told me were both miracles," she said.

Her treatment continued for more than a decade, until suddenly, in 2024, she received a phonecall from a doctor saying her chemotherapy was stopping.

"He didn't have any reason as to why. He told me Ian Brown had retired - this was the first I'd heard of it," Jones said.

Any questions would be answered by her new oncologist, she was told, but she was not given any name.

"I didn't know what to do, where to turn, who to talk to because I had no support from the hospital during that time," she said.

In May 2025, after independent analysis by neurosurgeons and radiologists, on behalf of her lawyers, she was told she had never had cancer of the brain at all.

She had actually been suffering from a tumefactive demyelination - an inflammation which is usually treated by neurologists who would prescribe strong steroids.

Jones got the news on a video call with her solicitors and the experts.

"When we found out there were just tears in everyone's eyes," said Tinsley, who is representing many of the patients.

The RPC review, which did not name Prof Ian Brown but referred to "Dr Y", found out of the 20 cases reviewed, 15 were "unsatisfactory overall". The consultant did not participate in the review.

There was "scant evidence" of the understanding and documentation of the risks of taking the drug, the review team found.

The preliminary findings said there was "insufficient clinical curiosity" in some cases and a lack of collaboration with multidisciplinary team colleagues, allowing potential diagnostic errors to persist.

Jones described the findings as "chilling".

"It's not just about what he's done, it's about how they let him act on his own for so long," she added.

"It's almost like he was running his own show and no one was there to monitor what he was doing."

A UHCW spokesperson said all affected patients had been reviewed by senior clinicians, "with appropriate care plans put in place".

"We are also undertaking an independent review of our speak-up processes, led by an independent party, to ensure staff feel fully supported and confident in raising any concerns.

"The trust will assess the full RCP review when it is published and will take further appropriate action based on its findings.

"We want to reassure our community that patient safety, experience and wellbeing remain our top priorities," the trust added.

articles.title: September reset: Why now is the time to start a new routine and how to stick to it
articles.summary: It's the month when many of us embark on a new chapter so here's how to start strong and keep the good habits.
articles.body:
The lazy hazy days of summer may feel like a distant memory as September shifts our energy back to business and forward to new adventures.

It's the month when many of us embark on a new chapter, whether it's university, college or a new job or simply getting back to work and the school run.

It's also the time that "September Reset" trends on social media - the kind, chill sister of New Year's Resolutions. Instead of strict rules and major life overhauls, creators are sharing small changes aimed at finishing the year strong.

"It's getting ahead of the game," says Cami Sophia, 24, who has shared her new rituals on TikTok. Here's why September could be the right time for a reset and how to create a new routine that lasts.

For Cami, a content creator and podcast host from Northampton, September spells the end of summer spontaneity and a time to restore order.

"If you've been away for the summer you've probably not had a massive routine," she says. "And if you're a parent, then you've got kids at home and it's just a bit more chaotic," she says.

September feels like "back to school...getting back into your own rhythm", she adds.

It is the perfect time to "get everything sorted", she says "So when you get to January you're not trying to do everything at once.

For Bas Verplanken, professor emeritus of social psychology at the University of Bath, September is a chance to "reorient yourself".

He says his research suggests people who experienced a big change such as moving house "were more responsive to an intervention aimed at promoting sustainable behaviours" than comparable people who had not moved house.

"It's really an exciting way of looking at disruption," he told Chris and Xand van Tulleken on their What's Up Docs? podcast.

If your daily commute or school run works for you then relax back into them.

"But if there are alternative ways of doing things, explore it, this is the time to do it, and to make those changes," says Verplanken.

TikTok is awash with videos on how to "lock in" starting small - declutter your room, clear out your wardrobe, go for a walk, start a new book.

But Cami warns against videos showing spreadsheets of radical changes.

"It's very easy to look at all of these things and what you should apparently be doing and get really overwhelmed," she says.

Cami starts her own reset by "looking at the goals I set at the start of the year and see what I actually still want to do - and then what I need to do to get from A to B".

Then she recommends picking three small "non-negotiables".

"They could be to have fruit with your breakfast, have veg with dinner and have a glass of water before you drink coffee," she says.

She advises small changes that require little effort - she is getting back into sleep patterns by setting alarms.

Cami says planning is key - something she does on a Sunday morning.

"I go, okay, these are my meals for the week. These are my workouts for the week. Even plan your outfits for the work day if you really want to because it saves you time," she says.

Then she takes steps to "limit the choices" she has to stray from her routine.

"I will meal prep three days worth of overnight oats. Naturally, I'm going to grab those in the morning because they are made and ready. I've removed the friction of grabbing a quick meal or not having any breakfast."

Verplanken agrees the secret to making new habits that last is setting yourself up so that your new behaviours are the easiest option for reaching your goal.

He advises designing a routine where your habits can become "effortless".

"They are specific plans of where, when, and what you will do," he says.

"Let's say, losing weight, you can think when I go to the supermarket, I'm going to look specifically each time [at] the fat and sugar content [of food]. It's a very specific plan."

This means making the right choices when are facing the food shelf happen automatically "because you have already planned the situation in which you have to act".

If this is done frequently, Verplanken says it becomes "extremely effective" to turn these habits into your routine.

articles.title: The Pitt is up for 25 Emmys - but the show's biggest fans are real-life doctors
articles.summary: Those in the medical profession say the HBO Max show about a US hospital emergency room is the most realistic medical drama yet.
articles.body:
It's a familiar sight: a crowded waiting room, trolleys in corridors, stressed doctors and nurses. But this isn't a typical A&E unit in the NHS, it's a Hollywood set with actors recreating the drama of an emergency department for TV series The Pitt.

And among its biggest fans are real-life doctors.

"We finally feel validated for everything we go through every day," says Dr Tony Cirillo, President of the American College of Emergency Physicians.

On Monday, The Pitt could become this year's most decorated series at the Emmys, America's most coveted TV honours, with 25 nominations.

Doctors and others in the medical profession say, for them, it's the most realistic medical drama yet - which is why they love it.

The series covers the life and work of the staff of Pittsburgh's Trauma Medical Centre, with each episode representing an hour of a day and there are 15 in each series.

A constant thread through each episode is the noise, the pace of activity and the constant demands on the staff who never seem to get a break. Complex procedures and life-saving interventions are shown in graphic, and often, gory detail.

The lead character Dr Michael Robinavitch, known as Dr Robby, is a hardened and highly experienced emergency medicine consultant (in US hospitals a senior emergency attending physician).

Played by Noah Wyle, previously in the cast of mid-90s medical drama ER, he is an executive producer as well as part of the writing team, which includes qualified doctors.

Wyle was invited to take part in a platform discussion at a prestigious conference with more than 6,000 emergency medicine experts in the audience.

"People came up to him and, as opposed to actors and athletes where they say they are amazing or love their work, people just said thank you to him," Cirillo says.

"The Pitt is more than just a good TV show – the term I use is validation."

Social and ethical issues are often reflected. A stressed daughter who is caring for her sick mother leaves her in the emergency department and then can't be found.

There are anguished conversations with parents who are desperate for their child to be kept alive, despite doctors saying there is no hope.

Health inequalities are highlighted, with some patients struggling with the payments required in the US health system.

Long waits and patient frustration are obvious shades of the NHS.

And, based on our conversations, the series has become more popular in the UK with medics.

Doctors seem ready to watch even in weeks when they have had punishing days or nights in A&E.

One of them is Dr Fiona Hunter, vice president of the Royal College of Emergency Medicine in Scotland.

"I wouldn't do it straight after a shift," she said. "We all need to decompress and debrief what we have experienced.

"But in between shifts, when I have got downtime, it's watchable, relatable. It makes me feel other people might get it."

North Wales consultant Dr Rob Perry is another fan.

"I think it is reassuring when you see people portraying doctors and nurses in a similar job to your own and, though its not in the UK, they are doing their level best to give the best care they can," he said.

'A very common problem around the world'

Doctors we spoke to do point out that each episode of The Pitt brings together several urgent trauma cases which typically might be spread across 24 hours or more.

But Prof Damian Roland, a practising emergency medicine consultant, notes that the drama does illustrate wider health challenges.

He thinks it puts the problems of the NHS in perspective.

"Virtually every emergency department in the world at the moment has not enough space to see patients," he says.

"It's a very common theme in The Pitt about the central character arguing with hospital management saying 'I need more flow, you can't just leave these patients here' – that's a very common problem."

"In my work in the NHS, its very much we all work for one another and I like that we represent that on the show," says Sarah Tosh, a senior NHS nurse who is the series medical adviser.

"In The Pitt they've got a bit about the characters' day-to-day life, but it's more about their medicine, which patient they are doing and what they are going on to next."

One of the stars of The Pitt, Gerran Howell, was born and brought up in South Wales.

With other actors he was put through a medical boot camp for speed learning of medical techniques and jargon. This included training on dummies and CPR practice.

In a BBC Wales interview he was asked if he would like to train to be a doctor.

"I have such a newfound respect for the medical profession. It's maybe made me realise that I don't know how I would do this. I will stick to acting."

Howell is nominated for an outstanding supporting actor award at the Emmys.

The winners will be announced on 14 September at a ceremony in Los Angeles.

The Pitt is available to stream on HBO Max in the UK.

articles.title: Buckingham Palace works uncover trove of everyday items dating back to 1800s
articles.summary: A collection of historic, forgotten items have been found during the restoration of the London royal residence.
articles.body:
A pair of battered, hobnailed boots and a newspaper cutting dating back nearly 140 years are among a trove of everyday objects unearthed during restoration work at Buckingham Palace.

The misplaced items are thought to belong to staff who worked at the palace decades ago, and were found by workers carrying out the £369m refurbishment.

A ticket for a "whist drive" - a card game event hosted by the palace on 14 April 1949 - was found embedded in a lump of brick.

Several betting slips, a bottle of Schweppes Still Malvern English Spring Water, an empty Silk Cut cigarette carton and a newspaper article about the gang jailed for the 1963 Great Train Robbery were also found under floorboards.

King and Queen will not live in Buckingham Palace after renovations

King becomes first monarch to reveal tax bill as royal public funding to double to £100m

The royal residence in London is undergoing a 10-year refurbishment plan - funded through a temporary increase in the Sovereign Grant, which pays for the official duties of the royals. It is due to be completed in March.

Ageing cables, lead pipes, wiring and boilers are set to be replaced - many for the first time in 60 years - following concerns about potential fire and water damage.

Until now, many of the items have remained hidden within the building's infrastructure.

Among the discoveries was a typed schedule detailing Queen Elizabeth II's plans to host a diplomatic reception in her Silver Jubilee year of 1977.

It revealed the monarch would work the room in a "clockwise direction", and that aides were asked to encourage the 350 British guests to mingle with the diplomats at the annual gathering.

"The British guests will be distributed throughout the State Rooms, except the Music Room and West Gallery, where they should be encouraged to talk to the Diplomats," the sheet reads.

Blank Littlewoods Football Pool betting slips from 1957 and a scrap of West End theatre listings from The Standard newspaper in 1889 were also found, alongside fragments of Minton decorative ceramic tiles from a fireplace hearth, with the design dated to around the mid-1800s.

A pewter tankard, a wooden junction box and a faded box containing six Christmas cards were included in the haul.

Examples of electrical wire covered with vulcanised Indian rubber cabling were found. It was replaced as priority when the restoration began as it posed the greatest risk of fire to the building.

Also discovered were pages from the Daily Express newspaper in 1966 detailing the "maximum security" prison where the Great Train Robbers were incarcerated.

The article had pictures of Durham Prison, revealing that "the men who were found guilty of stealing a fortune in mailbags spend their week stitching them for nine shillings".

Meanwhile, the whist drive ticket, priced at 6d or sixpence, would have taken place during the reign of King Charles III's grandfather, George VI, hosted by the Buckingham palace social club.

King Charles and Queen Camilla are currently residing in Clarence House, which stands beside St James's Palace and was once the Queen Mother's home.

They will not live in Buckingham Palace after the refurbishment is completed.

The decision was also taken to allow greater public access to the landmark, officials said. The landmark may now also be able to open for a longer period, generating more income.

The King will continue to host a range of events at the palace, from state banquets and garden parties to receptions and audiences with the prime minister and new ambassadors.

articles.title: Emmy Awards 2026: What to expect from the ceremony and how to watch
articles.summary: Beef stars Oscar Isaac and Carey Mulligan are among the nominees at the ceremony in Los Angeles.
articles.body:
Beef, Hacks, Pluribus and The Pitt are a few of the TV shows nominated at this year's Emmy Awards, which take place on Monday in Los Angeles.

Widow's Bay, DTF St Louis, Slow Horses, The Bear and Abbott Elementary are also competing for prizes at the ceremony, which is seen as the US television industry's most prestigious event.

Actors nominated for trophies include Zendaya, Noah Wyle, Sarah Snook and Colman Domingo, while Matthew Rhys, Carey Mulligan and Jack Lowden are among the British nominees.

But several big shows are not represented - viral sensation Heated Rivalry is not eligible for the Emmys, while there is a weaker presence for the final series of Euphoria and Stranger Things.

Here's everything you need to know about this year's Emmy Awards.

The Emmys split their nominations into three overarching categories: comedy, drama and limited or anthology series.

Best drama is generally seen as the night's most prestigious prize, and last year's winner The Pitt is back to defend its title following its second series.

The acclaimed medical drama also has eight individual acting nominations, including one for its star, Noah Wyle.

Other dramas nominated include Pluribus, Slow Horses, The Diplomat and Game of Thrones prequel A Knight Of The Seven Kingdoms .

Over in the comedy categories, Hollywood satire Hacks is predicted by many to continue its hugely successful Emmys streak following its fifth and final season.

The show's expected wins could include acting prizes for its two stars, Jean Smart and Hannah Einbinder.

Smart already has four Emmys for Hacks, having never lost for her performances in the previous four seasons. Another win would bring her total Emmy tally to eight, tying the record held by Julia Louis-Dreyfus and Cloris Leachman.

Possible challengers in the comedy categories include Widow's Bay, Shrinking, Abbott Elementary and Nobody Wants This.

Elsewhere, the second season of Netflix's Beef could be a strong contender in the limited or anthology series category, and win acting prizes for its stars Carey Mulligan and Oscar Isaac.

But it faces strong competition from shows such as All Her Fault, The Beast in Me and DTF St Louis , which had a particularly strong showing at last week's Creative Arts Emmys.

British nominees alongside Mulligan include Riz Ahmed (Bait), Rufus Sewell (The Diplomat), Kate O’Flynn (Widow’s Bay) and Gary Oldman and Jack Lowden (both for Slow Horses).

And many are keeping a particularly close eye on Welsh star Matthew Rhys, who is nominated in two different lead actor categories - for comedy Widow's Bay and limited series The Beast in Me.

The buzziest show of the last year, Heated Rivalry , starring Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams, is missing from this year's Emmy nominations.

The ice hockey romance did not qualify because it is a fully financed Canadian production, without the US involvement needed to be recognised at the Emmys.

Its ineligibility puzzled many who remember Schitt's Creek, a show more Canadian than maple cream cookies, dominating the Emmys in 2021.

But that qualified because of its financial and broadcast partnerships in the US, including creator and star Dan Levy's own American-based production company.

Heated Rivalry will instead be eligible to compete for the next International Emmys, which take place in New York in November.

Meanwhile, two other viral shows popular with younger audiences that were eligible for the US ceremony had a weaker-than-expected showing in the nominations list.

The final series of Stranger Things is absent in the top categories this year, scoring only seven nominations in technical categories.

And despite its star-packed cast, Euphoria 's last season managed only one acting nomination for former winner Zendaya.

What changes have been made to the ceremony?

Two categories have been merged this year - best talk series and best scripted variety series are now combined in a single category: outstanding variety series.

That means chat show hosts such as Jimmy Kimmel will compete against topical variety shows such as Saturday Night Live and Last Week Tonight With John Oliver.

Some other categories were also moved out of the telecast this year and have already been handed out, in an effort to revitalise the ceremony and leave more time for entertainment.

For example, best supporting actor and actress in a limited series, usually awarded during the main ceremony, were moved to the earlier Creative Arts Emmys ceremonies this year.

The total number of trophies awarded on the big night has been reduced from 26 to 19, a move the Academy said was intended to leave room for more musical performances, comedic sketches and unexpected acceptance speeches.

The ceremony will begin at 17:00 PT / 20:00 ET on Monday, taking place at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles.

US viewers can watch the Emmy Awards live on NBC or on streaming service Peacock.

In the UK, it will start at 01:00 BST on Tuesday morning, but no British broadcaster is scheduled to show it live.

However, there will be overnight coverage on the BBC News website throughout the red carpet and ceremony.

Winners at last weekend's Creative Arts Emmys included DTF St Louis stars Linda Cardellini and David Harbour, who won best supporting actress and actor in a limited series.

Betty Gilpin (Widow's Bay), Ernest Harden Jr (The Pitt), Shailene Woodley (Paradise) and the late Rob Reiner (The Bear) all won prizes for their guest acting roles, while British star Julie Andrews won best voiceover performance for Bridgerton.

Other British winners included Alan Cumming, who won best reality host for the US version of The Traitors.

Remarkably Bright Creatures, a drama starring Sally Field and Lewis Pullman about a perceptive octopus who observes the staff in his aquarium, won best movie.

South Park won best animated series, Mr. Scorsese took best docuseries, Love on the Spectrum won best unstructured reality programme, and the Super Bowl Halftime Show Starring Bad Bunny won best variety special.

US actress Mariska Hargitay, star of Law and Order: Special Victims Unit, will host this year's Primetime Emmys ceremony.

Her hugely successful crime series, known as SVU, has been running since 1999, and continues to be popular with younger audiences who have discovered it on streaming services.

Hargitay has been Emmy nominated eight times herself for playing detective Olivia Benson, winning for lead actress in a drama series in 2006.

SVU is one of the longest-running TV dramas of all time and is set to reach its 600th episode when its 28th season airs this autumn.

And at last weekend's Creative Arts Emmys, Hargitay also won two prizes for her documentary My Mom Jayne, about her actress mother Jayne Mansfield, who died in a car accident when Hargitay was three.

"Bringing important stories into the light has been the heartbeat of my career," Hargitay said in a statement.

"It's my great honour to host the 78th Emmy Awards and celebrate this extraordinary community of storytellers.

"Whether it's an actor or a director, a costumer or a sound designer, we are all so privileged to take part in creating television that unites us."

articles.title: How to protect your laptop, phone and bike from thieves at uni
articles.summary: What should new students consider to keep your belongings safe and covered by insurance?
articles.body:
Laptops, phones and bikes are top of the shopping list for thieves as students head off to university, according to insurer Aviva.

They are the items most likely to be on student insurance claims - after being stolen from digs, cars, public transport and bars and restaurants.

But there are ways you can help keep them safe, and things to consider if you are planning to get insurance cover.

Get it wrong and it can be expensive, or possibly illegal.

The majority of student insurance claims are the result of theft, ahead of accidental damage, according to Aviva. The insurer declined to say what proportion of claims resulted in payouts.

"Laptops, computers and mobile phones play a vital role in student life, but they can also be attractive targets for opportunistic thieves due to their value and portability," said Steven Jackson, its home product manager.

Leaving really expensive and sentimental belongings back at home

Locking up valuables and keeping them out of sight when you're out

Staying vigilant - do you really need to leave your bag or laptop to reserve a café table or a spot in the library?

It is entirely the choice of an individual as to whether it is worth insuring belongings while off at university or college.

Car insurance is compulsory, says the Association of British Insurers (ABI), but you can choose whether it's worth insuring your bike or other items.

How to make sure you've got the correct cover

First, the ABI suggests checking if you are covered already. Some student halls might already include insurance, or your parents' policy might extend to you.

If not, there is the option of buying contents insurance.

"This type of policy covers the cost of replacing or repairing your possessions if they are damaged, destroyed or stolen - giving you peace of mind that you're protected should something go wrong," the ABI said.

You must check how much you're covered for and whether it's enough to replace everything, including the maximum value of a claim on a single item.

You can do this by creating an inventory of all of your contents, including clothes, electronics and furniture, and adding up the cost of replacing each item.

You might need to pay extra to cover a nice bike, or to cover items that you take out and about with you rather than leave in your accommodation.

And, if you're driving, make sure your insurer knows the car is kept somewhere new.

If it is your parents' car and you are now the main driver, you have to inform the insurer. It's illegal if you don't.

articles.title: Accused killers vanish after family massacre before manhunt ends hundreds of miles away
articles.summary: A deadly North Carolina shooting left two dead and two critically injured before suspects Camryn Moore and Cory Armstrong fled across state lines.
articles.body: A deadly shooting inside a North Carolina family home triggered an urgent search for two accused killers and an interstate manhunt that would end with another burst of gunfire. Gaston County Police officers responded to a home on Forbes Road at approximately 8:43 a.m. Thursday after receiving a report of gunfire inside the residence. Officers discovered four people suffering from gunshot wounds. Two were pronounced dead at the scene, while two others were rushed to CaroMont Regional Medical Center with life-threatening injuries. Police identified the two people killed as Victoria "Heather" Moore, 50, and Megan "Josiah" Bumgardner, 38. The two surviving victims remained in critical but stable condition Friday, according to police. 4 SHOT INSIDE NORTH CAROLINA HOME, 2 KILLED AS POLICE IDENTIFY PERSON OF INTEREST Detectives identified two residents of the home, Camryn Moore, 26, and Cory Armstrong, 29, as suspects in the bloodshed. WSOC-TV reported that Heather Moore was Camryn Moore’s mother and Bumgardner was her uncle. Police said they believed everyone involved knew one another and described the shooting as an isolated incident with no continuing threat to the Gaston County community. Investigators have not disclosed what may have triggered the violence. Camryn Moore and Armstrong allegedly fled Gaston County immediately after the shooting. By Thursday afternoon, detectives had obtained warrants charging each of them with two counts of first-degree murder and two counts of attempted first-degree murder. WATCH: DEPUTIES HUNT WANTED MAN THROUGH CORNFIELD AFTER HIGH-SPEED CHASE CAUGHT ON CAMERA The Gaston County Police Department enlisted the help of the U.S. Marshals Service Carolinas Regional Fugitive Task Force as investigators tracked the pair’s movements across multiple states overnight. SUSPECTED HUMAN SMUGGLERS LEAD COPS ON 100-MPH CHASE BEFORE BAILING AND ALLEGEDLY COMMITTING ARMED CARJACKING The search reached Ohio at approximately 8 a.m. Friday, when state troopers spotted the suspects’ vehicle outside Athens and attempted to pull it over, authorities said. Moore and Armstrong allegedly refused to stop, setting off a multi-county pursuit. The chase came to a violent end when their vehicle swerved to avoid spike strips deployed in the roadway and crashed, according to information provided to North Carolina investigators by Ohio authorities. Officers then reported hearing two gunshots coming from the wrecked vehicle. Law enforcement deployed a drone to look inside and discovered Moore and Armstrong dead. Authorities have not disclosed who fired the shots or officially announced the manner of their deaths. The Ohio State Highway Patrol is investigating the pursuit, crash and deaths. Back in Gastonia, neighbors were stunned by the violence that shattered their normally peaceful street. Loretta Forbes, whose husband’s grandfather built her home in 1914 and gave Forbes Road its name, told WSOC-TV that she knew the family living next door. "I just kept saying, ‘My God. Oh God,’ coming down the stairs," Forbes told the outlet. "They seem to be very nice people. It just shakes you up to think that could happen so close by." Forbes said she was praying for the family and searching for answers. "I want to know what’s happened," she said. "I want to know about the family." Jennifer Greene, a friend and co-worker of Heather Moore, drove to the home after Moore unexpectedly failed to report for her shift. SUSPECTED DUI DRIVER LEADS COPS ON WILD CHASE BEFORE DRAMATIC TAKEDOWN ON POPULAR CALIFORNIA BEACH "This was a tragic act of violence that resulted in the loss of multiple lives and left others critically injured," the Gaston County Police Department said. "Although the search for the suspects has ended, our investigation has not," police added. Fox News Digital reached out to the Gaston County Police Department and Ohio State Highway Patrol for additional information.

articles.title: WWE star Stephanie Vaquer captures Women's World Championship at Chile live event in surprising moment
articles.summary: Stephanie Vaquer stunned fans in Santiago by defeating Liv Morgan for the Women's World Championship after Becky Lynch's shocking referee turn.
articles.body: Professional wrestling is filled with hard-hitting and fast-paced action and when you mix in a storyline that fans can buy into, the emotional response can really make the sport something great. There’s always an ace that companies and promotions can play as well – unpredictability. The uncertain nature of what’s going to happen in the ring even if the outcome behind the curtain is so-called "pre-determined." COMPLETE PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE ON OUTKICK What happened on Saturday night in Santiago, Chile, was WWE at its best. It seemed like a routine house show on WWE’s tour of South America as some of its superstars prepare for a raucous "Monday Night Raw" in Mexico City at Arena CDMX. Stephanie Vaquer, who is from Chile and had the entire nation behind her, went up against Liv Morgan for the Women’s World Championship. House shows are untelevised events that occur outside of the main shows that WWE holds each week. Usually, champions put their titles on the line or have matches against rivals with little to no consequence to the storylines they’re telling when fans tune in on Mondays, Tuesdays and Fridays. Saturday night changed all that when Vaquer defeated Morgan with Becky Lynch as the special guest referee. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Morgan was upset with Lynch’s officiating and began to push her in the ring. She then slapped her across the face. Morgan turned her attention back to Vaquer and was met with a thrust kick. Vaquer tried to finish off Morgan but the New Jersey native countered and quickly hit Vaquer with an Oblivion. Lynch went to count and as she hit two, she stopped and gave Morgan double birds. Vaquer took advantage. She went on the offensive and finished Morgan off with the Vaquer Inferno from the top rope. She pinned Morgan and the crowd in Santiago exploded. It is the second reign for Vaquer. She initially won the vacated title at Wrestlepalooza against Iyo Sky last September. She held the championship for 210 days before Morgan won it at WrestleMania 42. Morgan’s latest reign comes to an end at 147 days. While Vaquer celebrated with some women on the Raw roster, there are sharks swimming around her to get a chance at the belt. Lynch is among those who will immediately step into the title picture.
